C005.object: short-term adherence to intermittent fasting regimens among users with high baseline impulsivity
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Reminders and tracking features in fasting apps short-term adherence to intermittent fasting regimens among users with high baseline impulsivity]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial comparing adherence rates in high-impulsivity users assigned to app-based reminders vs. no-reminder control over 4 weeks — Directly tests causal effect of reminders on short-term adherence in the target subgroup, providing high internal validity for the disputed hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) study tracking daily impulsivity states and app engagement in first-time intermittent fasting users — Captures real-time fluctuations in impulsivity and response to reminders, clarifying whether the effect is moderated by trait vs. state impulsivity within the specified temporal scope.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of digital health interventions for dietary adherence, with subgroup analysis by impulsivity measures — Synthesizes existing evidence across studies to assess consistency of the moderation effect and identify potential confounding variables, strengthening or refuting the hypothesis at a broader level.

scope.domain: behavioral adherence during first 4 weeks, moderated by trait impulsivity

C006.subject: Reminders and tracking features in fasting apps
C006.object: user motivation for long-term adherence to intermittent fasting regimens
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Reminders and tracking features in fasting apps user motivation for long-term adherence to intermittent fasting regimens]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal randomized controlled trial comparing fasting app usage with and without reminders/tracking features, measuring adherence at 3, 6, and 12 months — Directly tests whether these features diminish motivation over the first 6 months versus a control, providing causal evidence for the disputed hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of digital health intervention studies on habit formation and motivation decay in dietary adherence apps — Synthesizes existing findings on how tracking and reminders affect intrinsic motivation and long-term adherence, helping contextualize the hypothesis within broader behavioral science evidence.

[PATH:theoretical] Self-determination theory framework applied to fasting app design: analysis of autonomy, competence, and relatedness in user experience — Provides a theoretical basis to predict that excessive reminders and tracking may undermine intrinsic motivation by reducing perceived autonomy, which could explain the hypothesized diminishing effect.

scope.domain: behavioral adherence beyond initial engagement period

C007.object: risk of dropout and rebound weight gain in intermittent fasting compared to apps without gamification
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Obsessive self-monitoring via fasting apps with gamified rewards risk of dropout and rebound weight gain in intermittent fasting compared to apps without gamification]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial comparing dropout rates and 12-month weight trajectories in intermittent fasting users of gamified apps vs. non-gamified tracking apps — Directly tests the causal effect of gamified self-monitoring on long-term adherence and weight regain, addressing the core hypothesis with high internal validity.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal cohort study using app analytics (e.g., daily log-in frequency, reward redemption patterns) to predict discontinuation and weight rebound in intermittent fasting populations over 6–12 months — Provides real-world behavioral data linking obsessive self-monitoring (measured via engagement metrics) to dropout and rebound, offering ecological validity and potential for dose-response analysis.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of gamification effects on adherence and weight outcomes in digital health interventions for weight loss, with subgroup analysis by fasting protocols — Synthesizes existing evidence across studies to assess whether gamification consistently increases dropout and rebound in intermittent fasting contexts, controlling for confounding variables.
